standing_assumptions:
Setting, notation and standing assumptions, as printed. Every passage was read from the rendered page images. Article pages are those of Political Analysis 31 (2023), with the PDF page in parentheses; the supplement is the publisher's Supporting Information (publisher-supplement.pdf, 5 pp., printed and PDF page numbers coincide).
[Notation: Section 2, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “Before we proceed, we introduce some notation. Let $n$ be the number of observations. Let $k$ be the number of variables (columns) in the dataset. Let $M_{ij}$ be a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th variable in the $i$th row is missing. For notational convenience, we will let $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$ represent the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$ $(M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$.”
[Assumption 1, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “All rows of the data $((M_{11}, \ldots, M_{1k}), \ldots, (M_{n1}, \ldots, M_{nk}))$ are mutually independent.”
[Assumption 2, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ and • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, k\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = 0) > 0$.”
[The quantity $p_{all}$: Section 2.1, p. 150 (PDF p. 2)] “We begin by application of elementary probability theory to yield the following finite-$n$ result. In words, this result establishes an exact lower bound on the probability that all rows of the data will suffer from some missingness. In such instances, listwise deletion would yield no usable data.” Lemma 3 then names $p_{all}$ as “the probability that listwise deletion removes all rows”.
[The sequence: pp. 150-151 (PDF pp. 2-3)] “We can now consider the asymptotic properties of listwise deletion, letting both $k$ and $n$ tend to infinity. To do so, we embed the above problem into a sequence. We let $k_n = f(n)$, where $f$ has range over the natural numbers, and allow $M_{ij,n}$ and therefore $q_{ij,n}$ to vary at each $n$. To ease exposition, we omit notational dependence on $n$.”
[Assumption 4, p. 151 (PDF p. 3)] “The number of covariates grows superlogarithmically in $n$, so that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{f(n)}{log(n)} = \infty$.” The next sentence: “Assumption 4 can be equivalently written in asymptotic shorthand notation as $k = \omega(\log n)$.”
[Reading fixed by the printed text and used in every target] $M_{ij} = 1$ means that entry $(i,j)$ is missing and $M_{ij} = 0$ that it is observed (the proof of Lemma 3, p. 154, treats $1 - \Pr(\mathbf{M}_{ik} = 0)$ as “the probability of a single observation containing at least one missing entry”). The event written $\mathbf{M}_{ij} = 0$ is $\{M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0\}$. Row $i$ is removed by listwise deletion when at least one of $M_{i1}, \ldots, M_{ik}$ equals 1, and $p_{all}$ is the probability that every one of the $n$ rows has at least one $j$ with $M_{ij} = 1$. $q_*$ is an upper bound on a probability of being observed. It is one constant, the same for every row and, along the sequence, for every $n$; the laws of the $M_{ij,n}$ may change with $n$ (this is the reading the validator fixed for P007-N002, which was not confirmed as an error). $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 1$ are integers; $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The symbol $q_{ij}$ is defined only inside the proof of Lemma 3 (p. 154).
[Supplement, Supporting Information A, p. 1] “Here we demonstrate the finite-$n$ implications of our findings. In the following figures, we plot figures for different values of an upper bound on the conditional probability of each data entry being observed $q_*$, the number of observations (rows) $n$, the number of variables (columns) $k$ and a sharp lower bound on $p_{all}$ denoted $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n$. $\underline{p_{all}}$ is the lowest possible (”best-case”) probability that listwise deletion removes all data.” And, same page: “By Lemma 3, we can compute $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^k)^n$.”
[Supplement, Supporting Information B, p. 3] “Let $n$ be the number of observations. Let $g$ be the number of variable groups in the dataset, within which all observations share an identical missingness pattern. We let $M_{ij}$ be a random indicator variable for whether or not the $j$th group in the $i$th row is missing. We use one indicator for each group due to the shared missingness. Similar to the previous setting, we use $\mathbf{M}_{ij}$ to represent the random vector collecting the missingness indicators up to variable $j$, $(M_{i1}, M_{i2}, \ldots, M_{ij})$. Let $k$ be the number of variables in the dataset. Note that, by construction, we know that $k \geq g$ since groups contain at least one variable.” [p. 4] Assumption 6: “All rows of the data $\left((M_{11}, ..., M_{1g}), ..., (M_{n1}, ..., M_{ng})\right)$ are mutually independent.” Assumption 7: “There exists a $q_* \in [0,1)$ such that for all $i$, • $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) \leq q_*$ • $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0|\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) \leq q_*$, for all $j \in \{2, \ldots, g\}$ such that $\Pr(\mathbf{M}_{i(j-1)} = \mathbf{0}) > 0$”. The sequence: “Similarly, we will embed the problem into a sequence $g_n = l(n)$, where $l$ has range over the natural numbers, and allow $M_{ij,n}$ and $q_{ij,n}$ to vary at each $n$. We omit the $n$ notation for simplicity.” Assumption 9: “The number of groups of covariates grows superlogarithmically in $n$, so that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{l(n)}{log(n)} = \infty$.”
[Application: Section 3, pp. 151-152 (PDF pp. 3-4)] “We applied mild preprocessing to these datasets: we removed country code variables, and in the case of the State Failure data, to apply the principle of charity, we removed 19 variables that exhibited 100% missingness.” [Section 3.1, p. 152 (PDF p. 4)] “To do so, we conducted 25,000 simulations in each of which we drew $k$ of the variables from each dataset (without replacement). We then recorded the number of rows of the data that survive listwise deletion. We then report the expected proportion of remaining data observed after listwise deletion, as well as the probability that all rows of the data exhibit some missingness. Note that, here, expected values and probabilities refer to the randomness induced by our random subsampling procedure, not any fundamental stochasticity giving rise to the underlying data.” So in the application the data are a fixed array of missing and observed cells, and the only randomness is the uniform draw of $k$ of its variables without replacement. Assumptions 1 and 2 play no part in the targets about the application (P007-T1, P007-T2, P007-T12, P007-T13).
Scope of the targets. Headline claims that are mathematical statements: P007-H1 (Lemma 3: P007-T14), P007-H2 (Proposition 5: P007-T16) and P007-H6 (Lemma 8 and Proposition 10: P007-T15 and P007-T17). P007-H3 (the finite-$n$ illustration of the bound), P007-H4 and P007-H5 (the two data illustrations) and P007-H7 (the conclusion) are numerical illustrations, simulation results or interpretive remarks, so they are not headline targets; the formal content of the findings that touch P007-H3 and P007-H5 is in the targets below. Confirmed errors with mathematical content, each with a corrected-statement target: P007-E010 (Moderate; Table 1's State Failure average and the threshold “more than three variables”: exact refutation P007-T1, correction P007-T2, statement as printed P007-T13); P007-E003 (Minor; the printed proofs of Lemmas 3 and 8 and of Propositions 5 and 10: P007-T3 to P007-T6); P007-E005 (Minor; the Figure 4 paragraph of the supplement: P007-T7, P007-T8); P007-E006 (Minor; “upper bound” and the caption of Figure 5: P007-T9, P007-T10); P007-E004 (Minor; “i.i.d.” for Assumption 1: P007-T11); P007-E014 (Minor; its established part is the same stale Table 1 average: P007-T12). Confirmed errors that are not targets, because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P007-E009 (Moderate; the analysed file is the QoG Basic dataset and not the Standard dataset that is cited, a matter of data provenance, and every QoG number stands for the deposited file); P007-E001 (the glmnet software example); P007-E013 (a garbled reference entry); within P007-E004, the misprint “out” for “our”; within P007-E014, the behaviour of the is.na mask on empty Stata strings (a property of the code whose effect on the State Failure data was not established). Not targets because they are not rated as errors: P007-E002 and P007-N001 (clarity notes), P007-N002, P007-N004, P007-N005 and P007-N006 (not confirmed), P007-N003 (undetermined), P007-N007 (out of scope).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proofs of Proposition 5 and Proposition 10, third paragraph (the Bernoulli step), as repaired. The statements of the two propositions are unchanged
canonical_claim.location: p. 154 (PDF p. 6), Appendix: Proofs, Proof of Proposition 5, paragraph beginning “Since $q_* \in (0,1)$ and $k = f(n)$”; Supplement p. 4 (foot) and p. 5, Proof of Proposition 10, paragraph beginning “Since $q_* \in (0,1)$ and $k = l(n)$”
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 154 (PDF p. 6), Proof of Proposition 5] “Since $q_* \in (0,1)$ and $k = f(n) \geq_* 1$, $-q_*^{f(n)} > -1$ and $1 - q_*^{f(n)} \leq 1$. By Bernoulli's Inequality, since $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $(1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n \geq_* 1 + n(-q_*^{f(n)}) = 1 - nq_*^{f(n)}$. Thus $1 - nq_*^{f(n)} \leq (1 - q_*^{f(n})^n \leq 1$ in the common domain $n \in \mathbb{N}$.” [Printed, Supplement pp. 4-5, Proof of Proposition 10] “Since $q_* \in (0,1)$ and $k = l(n) \geq_* 1$, $-q_*^{l(n)} > -1$ and $1 - q_*^{l(n)} \leq 1$. By Bernoulli's Inequality, since $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $(1 - q_*^{l(n)})^n \geq_* 1 + n(-q_*^{l(n)}) = 1 - nq_*^{l(n)}$. Thus $1 - nq_*^{l(n)} \leq (1 - q_*^{l(n})^n \leq 1$ in the common domain $n \in \mathbb{N}$.” In both passages the relation is printed twice with a subscript star, $\geq_*$, and the middle term of the last display is printed with the closing parenthesis of the exponent missing, $(1 - q_*^{f(n})^n$ and $(1 - q_*^{l(n})^n$.
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P007-E003, prior_correction.corrected_text), the part on the propositions, verbatim] “Bernoulli gives 1-nq_*^h<=(1-q_*^h)^n<=1. For fixed 0<q_*<1 and h/log n tending to infinity, nq_*^h tends to zero; for q_*=0 the endpoint is immediate. Therefore p_all tends to 1. Replace the comma lists with products, remove stars on >=, balance superscript parentheses, write g=l(n) on supplement page 4, and up to group j on supplement page 3.” [Sol's smallest repair, the sentence on the endpoint] “Before the proposition logarithm argument explicitly dispatch q_*=0 using Lemma 3/8.”
[The paragraph as corrected] “Since $q_* \in (0,1)$ and $k = f(n) \geq 1$, $-q_*^{f(n)} > -1$ and $1 - q_*^{f(n)} \leq 1$. By Bernoulli's Inequality, since $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $(1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n \geq 1 + n(-q_*^{f(n)}) = 1 - nq_*^{f(n)}$. Thus $1 - nq_*^{f(n)} \leq (1 - q_*^{f(n)})^n \leq 1$ in the common domain $n \in \mathbb{N}$.” In the supplement the same, with $g = l(n)$ in place of $k = f(n)$ and $l(n)$ in place of $f(n)$ throughout.
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
(a) For every real $q$ with $0 \leq q < 1$ and all integers $h \geq 1$ and $n \geq 1$: $-q^h > -1$; $1 - q^h \leq 1$; $(1 - q^h)^n \geq 1 + n(-q^h) = 1 - nq^h$ (Bernoulli's inequality, with the ordinary relation $\geq$); and therefore $1 - nq^h \leq (1 - q^h)^n \leq 1$, where the exponent of $q$ in the middle term is $h$, that is $f(n)$, respectively $l(n)$.
(b) In the setting and under the hypotheses (A1) and (A2) of P007-T5, with $h \geq 1$: $1 - nq_*^h \leq (1 - q_*^h)^n \leq p_{all} \leq 1$, that is, $0 \leq 1 - p_{all} \leq nq_*^h$.
(c) [The endpoint, which the printed proofs omit when they take the logarithm of $q_*$.] If $q_* = 0$ and $h \geq 1$ then $p_{all} = 1$ (P007-T5 (a)). The identity $nq_*^h = e^{\log n + h\log q_*}$, on which the printed limit argument rests, is used only for $0 < q_* < 1$ (and $n \geq 1$), where it holds.
(d) [$g$ for $k$ in the proof of Proposition 10.] The quantity equal to $l(n)$ is the number of groups, $g_n = l(n)$, and (a) and (b) are applied with $h = g_n$. The printed “$k = l(n)$” is not an identity of the grouped setting, in which only $k \geq g$ holds: with $g_n = l(n) = n$ groups of two variables each, $k_n = 2n \neq l(n)$ for every $n \geq 1$ (at $n = 2$: $g = 2$, $k = 4$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [pp. 150-151] $k_n = f(n)$ and Assumption 4; [Supplement pp. 3-4] $g$, $k \geq g$, $g_n = l(n)$ and Assumption 9; all as transcribed in standing_assumptions. $\mathbb{N}$ is read as the positive integers (the number of observations). $p_{all}$, (A1), (A2) and $h$ as in P007-T5.
canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair (“remove the stars on >=, balance the f(n)/l(n) superscripts, change k=l(n) to g=l(n) on supplement page 4 [...] Before the proposition logarithm argument explicitly dispatch q_*=0 using Lemma 3/8”) and the sections “Bernoulli sandwich, proved explicitly” and “General proof of Propositions 5 and 10, including q_*=0” of the validator's derivation; part (d) is its witness D (exact_check.txt: “Grouped-index check”). These are the finite-$n$ steps of the two proofs; the limits are the headline targets P007-T16 and P007-T17, which list (a) to (c) among their finite lemmas. What the validator did not find: no value of $\log 0$ is computed on the page (the printed logarithm argument is stated for $q_* \in (0,1)$); the endpoint $q_* = 0$ is simply not treated in the printed proofs of the propositions, and it follows at once from the lemmas. The prior round located the line “$k = l(n)$” on Supplement p. 5; it is printed at the foot of p. 4. Part (a) holds for $h \geq 0$ and $n \geq 0$ except for the strict inequality $-q^h > -1$, which needs $h \geq 1$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supporting Information A, the two paragraphs on Figure 4 (“the smallest possible $k$”; “we need only $k = 33$”; “we need $k = 952$”; “ensuring that $p_{all} \leq 0.5, 0.99$”) and the caption of Figure 4. The witnesses are the validator's and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. 2 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 2), Supporting Information A, paragraphs beginning “Figure 4 illustrates” and “With more missingness”, and Figure 4; not in the article PDF
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, Supplement p. 2, Supporting Information A] “Figure 4 illustrates, for a given $n, q_*$, how large $k$ can be while still ensuring that $p_{all} \leq 0.5, 0.99$. We compute this using the result from Lemma 3, $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^k)^n$. Since $(1 - q_*^k)^n$ is strictly increasing in $k$, solving for equality $p_{all} = (1 - q_*^k)^n$ we will get the smallest possible $k$ for each $\underline{p_{all}}$ that $k = \left\lfloor \frac{\log(1 - \underline{p_{all}}^{1/n})}{\log(q_*)} \right\rfloor$. We present two subfigures: with $\underline{p_{all}} = 0.5$ for the first subfigure and $\underline{p_{all}} = 0.99$ for the second subfigure, and we plot the $k$ against the $n$ for three different upper bounds $q_* = 0.75, 0.90, 0.99$.” Next paragraph: “With more missingness, $q_* = 0.75, 0.90$, even relatively small $k$ can yield missingness of $\underline{p_{all}}$. For example, even with $n = 10,000$ and $q_* = 0.75$ we need only $k = 33$ to have a 50% probability that all rows will be missing. However, when missingness is very low, $k$ needs to be very large to cause all data to be missing. For example, with $n = 10,000$ and $q_* = 0.99$, we need $k = 952$ to have a 50% probability that all rows will be missing.” Plot titles: “Largest k such that probability all data missing is ≤ 0.50” and “Largest k such that probability all data missing is ≤ 0.99”. Subcaptions: “(a) $p_{all} \leq 0.5$” and “(b) $p_{all} \leq 0.99$”. Caption: “Figure 4. Largest $k$ such that $p_{all} \leq 0.5, 0.99$ plotted against $n$ and $q_*$.” (The underlines are as printed: $p_{all}$ carries no underline in the first sentence, in “solving for equality $p_{all} = (1 - q_*^k)^n$”, in the subcaptions and in the caption.)
[Counterexamples. Validator's witnesses; not in the paper.] Throughout, $B(k) = (1 - q_*^k)^n$ is the printed $\underline{p_{all}}$, and the “equal-probability model” is the law under which all $n \cdot k$ indicators $M_{ij}$ are independent with $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0) = q_*$; it satisfies Assumptions 1 and 2 with this $q_*$ and has $p_{all} = B(k)$ exactly.
(a) [Against “the smallest possible $k$” and “solving for equality”.] Take $n = 1$, $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$ and the target $\underline{p_{all}} = \frac{1}{2}$. Then $B(2) = 1 - \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{7}{16} < \frac{1}{2} < \frac{37}{64} = 1 - \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3 = B(3)$. The real solution $r = \log\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)/\log\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)$ of $1 - \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^r = \frac{1}{2}$ satisfies $2 < r < 3$, so the printed formula gives $k = \lfloor r \rfloor = 2$. This is the largest integer with $B(k) \leq \frac{1}{2}$; the smallest integer with $B(k) \geq \frac{1}{2}$ is $3$; and no integer $k$ solves the equality. In the equal-probability model the probability that all rows are missing at $k = 2$ is $\frac{7}{16} < \frac{1}{2}$.
(b) [Against “we need only $k = 33$ to have a 50% probability” and “we need $k = 952$ to have a 50% probability”.] With $n = 10000$: for $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$, $B(33) < \frac{1}{2} < B(34)$, where $B(33) = \left(1 - \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{33}\right)^{10000}$; for $q_* = \frac{99}{100}$, $B(952) < \frac{1}{2} < B(953)$, where $B(952) = \left(1 - \left(\frac{99}{100}\right)^{952}\right)^{10000}$. In the equal-probability model, $p_{all} = B(33)$, respectively $B(952)$: with 33, respectively 952, variables the probability that all rows are missing is below 50%, so Assumptions 1 and 2 do not give a 50% probability at those $k$. The first integers at which the lower bound reaches $\frac{1}{2}$ are 34 and 953.
(c) [Against “how large $k$ can be while still ensuring that $p_{all} \leq 0.5, 0.99$” and the caption and subcaptions, read for the probability $p_{all}$ itself and not for its lower bound.] (c1) $n = 1$, $k = 2$, $M_{11}$ and $M_{12}$ independent with $\Pr(M_{11} = 0) = \frac{3}{4}$ and $\Pr(M_{12} = 0) = \frac{1}{4}$: Assumptions 1 and 2 hold with $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$; $B(2) = \frac{7}{16} \leq \frac{1}{2}$ (and $k = 2$ is the printed floor for the target $\frac{1}{2}$); but $p_{all} = 1 - \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{13}{16} > \frac{1}{2}$. (c2) Target $\frac{99}{100}$: $n = 1$, $k = 16$, indicators independent with $\Pr(M_{11} = 0) = \frac{3}{4}$ and $\Pr(M_{1j} = 0) = \frac{1}{4}$ for $j = 2, \ldots, 16$: Assumptions 1 and 2 hold with $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$; $B(16) = \frac{4251920575}{4294967296} < \frac{99}{100} < B(17)$, so 16 is the printed floor; but $p_{all} = 1 - \frac{3}{4^{16}} = \frac{4294967293}{4294967296} > \frac{99}{100}$. (c3) At the printed parameters $n = 10000$, $k = 33$, $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$: all indicators independent with $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) = \frac{3}{4}$ and $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0) = \frac{1}{4}$ for $j = 2, \ldots, 33$: Assumptions 1 and 2 hold with $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$, and $p_{all} = \left(1 - \frac{3}{4^{33}}\right)^{10000} \geq 1 - \frac{30000}{4^{33}} > \frac{99}{100}$, while $B(33) < \frac{1}{2}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Supplement p. 1] $\underline{p_{all}}$, “a sharp lower bound on $p_{all}$”, “the lowest possible (”best-case”) probability that listwise deletion removes all data”; “By Lemma 3, we can compute $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^k)^n$”. [p. 150] Assumptions 1 and 2 and $p_{all}$ as in standing_assumptions; $q_*$ is “an upper bound on the conditional probability of each data entry being observed” (Supplement p. 1). $B(k)$ is the validator's notation for $(1 - q_*^k)^n$. Decimal values are read as exact rationals: $0.75 = \frac{3}{4}$, $0.99 = \frac{99}{100}$, $0.5 = \frac{1}{2}$, $10,000 = 10^4$.
canonical_claim.note: Sections 4 and 5 of the validator's derivation; verdict confirmed in part, upheld on recheck. What is refuted under the natural reading is the integer boundary: the plotted floor is called the smallest $k$, and 33 and 952 are said to give 50%: parts (a) and (b). Part (c) refutes only the literal reading in which the un-underlined $p_{all}$ is the actual probability; the validator judged the best-case intent clear from context (the titles, the formula and the definition on Supplement p. 1), so (c) shows why the underline matters and is not an error in the plotted quantity. What is not established: any error in the floor formula, the grid or the curves of Figure 4 (all 59,406 grid entries satisfy $B(k) < a < B(k+1)$), or that the actual probability cannot reach 50% at $k = 33$ or $952$ in some admissible law (in (c3) it exceeds 99%). For (b) the exact values are the rationals $\left(\frac{4^{33} - 3^{33}}{4^{33}}\right)^{10000}$ and $\left(\frac{100^{952} - 99^{952}}{100^{952}}\right)^{10000}$, with numerators of several hundred thousand, respectively several million, digits; the validator certifies the comparisons by rational interval arithmetic (certificates.json in the same folder): $B(33) \in [0.470753077326094,\ 0.470753077326095]$, $B(34) \in [0.568325557942055,\ 0.568325557942056]$, $B(952) \in [0.496887492657616,\ 0.496887492657617]$, $B(953) \in [0.500374984430253,\ 0.500374984430254]$. The margin at 953 is small ($3.7 \times 10^{-4}$), which is where a proof will need care. These values were recomputed to 60 significant digits when this list was fixed, and the small-case fractions exactly.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supporting Information A, the two paragraphs on Figure 4 and the caption, subcaptions and plot titles of Figure 4, as repaired by Sol
canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. 2 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 2), Supporting Information A; not in the article PDF
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] As transcribed in P007-T7: the paragraphs beginning “Figure 4 illustrates” and “With more missingness”, and the caption, subcaptions and plot titles of Figure 4 (Supplement p. 2).
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P007-E005, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Figure 4 shows, for each n and q_*, the largest nonnegative integer k for which the sharp lower bound \underline{p_{all}}=(1-q_*^k)^n does not exceed a, with a=0.5 or 0.99. Solving (1-q_*^r)^n=a gives r=\log(1-a^{1/n})/\log(q_*), and the plotted value is k=\lfloor r\rfloor. This calculation concerns the lowest possible all-deletion probability under Assumptions 1 and 2, not an upper bound on the actual probability. For n=10,000, the best-case probability is approximately 47.08% at q_*=0.75, k=33, and approximately 49.69% at q_*=0.99, k=952. The smallest integers making this lower bound at least 50% are respectively 34 and 953. Figure 4 caption: Largest k such that \underline{p_{all}}\leq0.5,0.99 plotted against n and q_*. Subcaptions: (a) \underline{p_{all}}\leq0.5; (b) \underline{p_{all}}\leq0.99. In both plot titles, replace 'probability all data missing' by 'lower bound on probability all data missing'.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
[Setting] An integer $n \geq 1$; real numbers $q_*$ and $a$ with $0 < q_* < 1$ and $0 < a < 1$; $B(k) = (1 - q_*^k)^n$ for integers $k \geq 0$; and $r = \dfrac{\log(1 - a^{1/n})}{\log(q_*)}$, with natural logarithms and $a^{1/n}$ the positive $n$th root.
(i) $B(0) = 0$, $0 \leq B(k) < 1$ and $B(k) < B(k+1)$ for every integer $k \geq 0$: $B$ is strictly increasing in $k$.
(ii) $r > 0$, and $r$ is the unique real $x \geq 0$ with $(1 - q_*^x)^n = a$. For every integer $k \geq 0$: $B(k) \leq a$ if and only if $k \leq r$; $B(k) \geq a$ if and only if $k \geq r$; $B(k) = a$ if and only if $k = r$.
(iii) $\max\{k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} : B(k) \leq a\} = \lfloor r \rfloor$, which is the plotted quantity: the largest such $k$, not the smallest. $\min\{k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} : B(k) \geq a\} = \lceil r \rceil$. The two integers are equal if and only if $r$ is an integer; otherwise $\lceil r \rceil = \lfloor r \rfloor + 1$ and $B(\lfloor r \rfloor) < a < B(\lceil r \rceil)$.
(iv) [What the two integers guarantee under the paper's assumptions.] For every law of $n$ rows and $k$ variables that satisfies Assumptions 1 and 2 with this $q_*$, if $k \geq \lceil r \rceil$ then $p_{all} \geq B(k) \geq a$. For every integer $k$ with $1 \leq k < r$ there is a law satisfying Assumptions 1 and 2 with this $q_*$ (all $n \cdot k$ indicators independent with $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0) = q_*$) for which $p_{all} = B(k) < a$. So $\lceil r \rceil$ is the smallest number of variables at which Assumptions 1 and 2 guarantee $p_{all} \geq a$, and $B(k)$ is the lowest value of $p_{all}$ that the assumptions allow. No bound of the form $p_{all} \leq a$ follows from $B(k) \leq a$ (P007-T7 (c)).

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, Supplement p. 2, last paragraph, continued on p. 3] “Our final numerical illustration considers an upper bound on the expected proportion of observations that are missing, $1 - q_*^k$, which does not depend on $n$. Figure 5 plots the expected proportion of data missing versus the number of variables $k$. We see the same qualititative relationship as before — as the number of variables increases, we have a very quick decline in the proportion of usable data. In comparison to Figure 3, the expected proportion of data missing tends faster to 1 for each $q_*$ considered as $k$ gets large, as it is equivalent to the special case for $\underline{p_{all}}$ when $n = 1$.” [Supplement p. 3] Plot title: “Lower bound on expected proportion of data missing”. Caption: “Figure 5. Lower bound of expected proportion of all rows missing ($\underline{p_{all}}$) plotted against values of $n$,$k$ and $q_*$.”
[Counterexample to the statement that $1 - q_*^k$ is an upper bound on the expected proportion of observations (rows) that are missing (removed by listwise deletion). Validator's witness; not in the paper.] Let $n = 2$, $k = 2$ and $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$. Let the four indicators $M_{11}, M_{12}, M_{21}, M_{22}$ be independent with $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) = \frac{3}{4}$ and $\Pr(M_{i2} = 0) = \frac{1}{2}$ for $i = 1, 2$. Let $D_i = 1$ if row $i$ has at least one missing entry and $D_i = 0$ otherwise, and $F_2 = \frac{1}{2}(D_1 + D_2)$, the proportion of rows removed.
(i) Assumption 1 holds: the two rows are independent.
(ii) Assumption 2 holds with $q_* = \frac{3}{4}$: $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) = \frac{3}{4} \leq \frac{3}{4}$, and $\Pr(M_{i2} = 0 \mid M_{i1} = 0) = \frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{3}{4}$ with $\Pr(M_{i1} = 0) > 0$. Moreover $\frac{3}{4}$ is the least $q_*$ for which Assumption 2 holds for this law.
(iii) Each row is complete with probability $\frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{8}$, so $\mathrm{E}[D_i] = \frac{5}{8}$ and $\mathrm{E}[F_2] = \frac{5}{8}$.
(iv) $1 - q_*^k = 1 - \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{7}{16} < \frac{5}{8}$. So $1 - q_*^k$ is not an upper bound on the expected proportion of rows removed.
(v) [The symbol in the caption.] In the same setting the quantity that the supplement denotes $\underline{p_{all}}$ is $(1 - q_*^k)^n = \left(\frac{7}{16}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{256} \neq \frac{7}{16}$, and the actual $p_{all}$ is $\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^2 = \frac{25}{64}$. For $n = 2$ the plotted quantity $1 - q_*^k$ is therefore not $\underline{p_{all}}$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] As transcribed in P007-T9: “Our final numerical illustration considers an upper bound on the expected proportion of observations that are missing, $1 - q_*^k$, which does not depend on $n$. Figure 5 plots the expected proportion of data missing versus the number of variables $k$.” Caption: “Figure 5. Lower bound of expected proportion of all rows missing ($\underline{p_{all}}$) plotted against values of $n$,$k$ and $q_*$.”
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P007-E006, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Our final numerical illustration considers a lower bound on the expected proportion of rows removed by listwise deletion, b_k=1-q_*^k, which does not depend on n. Figure 5 plots this lower bound versus the number of variables k. Figure 5. Lower bound b_k=1-q_*^k on the expected proportion of rows removed by listwise deletion, plotted against k for q_* in {0.75,0.90,0.99}.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
[Setting] Integers $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 1$; a probability space carrying indicators $M_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, $j = 1, \ldots, k$ ($1$ = missing); $s_{ij} = \Pr(M_{i1} = \cdots = M_{ij} = 0)$; $D_i = 1$ if row $i$ has at least one missing entry and $D_i = 0$ otherwise; $F_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} D_i$, the proportion of rows removed by listwise deletion; $b_k = 1 - q_*^k$.
[Hypothesis] Assumption 2: $q_* \in [0,1)$, and for every row $i$, $s_{i1} \leq q_*$ and $s_{ij}/s_{i(j-1)} \leq q_*$ for every $j \in \{2, \ldots, k\}$ with $s_{i(j-1)} > 0$. Assumption 1 (independence of the rows) is not assumed in (i) and (ii).
(i) $\mathrm{E}[D_i] = 1 - s_{ik} \geq 1 - q_*^k$ for every row $i$.
(ii) $\mathrm{E}[F_n] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - s_{ik}) \geq 1 - q_*^k = b_k$. The bound $b_k$ is a lower bound, and it does not depend on $n$.
(iii) [The bound is attained.] If all $n \cdot k$ indicators are independent with $\Pr(M_{ij} = 0) = q_*$, then Assumptions 1 and 2 hold with this $q_*$ and $\mathrm{E}[F_n] = b_k$.
(iv) [Relation to $\underline{p_{all}}$, the symbol printed in the caption.] $\underline{p_{all}} = (1 - q_*^k)^n = b_k^{\,n}$. For $n = 1$, $\underline{p_{all}} = b_k$. If $0 < q_* < 1$, $k \geq 1$ and $n \geq 2$, then $0 < b_k < 1$ and $\underline{p_{all}} = b_k^{\,n} < b_k$. So the curve of Figure 5 is $b_k$, a function of $k$ and $q_*$ alone, and it coincides with $\underline{p_{all}}$ only in the case $n = 1$ that the printed paragraph mentions or at the endpoint $q_* = 0$: for all integers $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 1$ and all $q_* \in [0,1)$, $\underline{p_{all}} = b_k$ if and only if $n = 1$ or $q_* = 0$.
